name: Body dysmorphia & mirror checking
lead: Body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) is a psychiatric condition marked by persistent preoccupation with perceived defects in appearance that are minor or unnoticeable to others, together with repetitive behaviours such as mirror checking, comparing, reassurance seeking and camouflaging [1][2][3]. Mirror checking, along with its opposite, mirror avoidance, is among the best-described of these behaviours [2][6]. Clinicians use the term body checking for the wider family of behaviours in which a person repeatedly gathers information about their own appearance [17].

For people working on how they look, the topic matters because the same attention that drives self-improvement can, in some people, become a loop that takes hours a day and distorts how they see their own face or body. Clinical sources describe the condition, its overlap with habits common in appearance-focused communities, and treatments reported to reduce the distress, so that people can tell a routine self-assessment from a pattern that clinicians recognise and treat [3][4][7].

In looksmaxxing communities, appearance scrutiny, self-rating and photo comparison are routine, and journalists and researchers have discussed whether these habits overlap with or worsen body dysmorphia. Wikipedia reports that critics describe looksmaxxing as linked to body dysmorphia and suicidal ideation [9]; Grokipedia likewise says self-rating and comparison are linked to body dysmorphia, depression and anxiety [8]. The articles do not present controlled studies establishing that looksmaxxing causes BDD.

Clinical reviews describe cognitive behavioural therapy and serotonin reuptake inhibitors as the best-supported treatments [3][4]. Reviews also report that people with BDD frequently seek cosmetic or dermatological treatment and that BDD is common in those settings [3][6][21].

paras: BDD involves preoccupation with a perceived flaw that takes up hours each day and causes distress or impaired functioning. The flaw may be imagined or a slight difference that the person sees as much larger [7]. DSM-5 (2013) reclassified the condition within the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders chapter and recognised muscle dysmorphia as a subtype [1][7].

The Italian psychiatrist Enrico Morselli described the condition as dysmorphophobia in the late nineteenth century. The American Psychiatric Association first included it in DSM-III in 1980 and named it body dysmorphic disorder in 1987 [7].

Enrico Morselli described dysmorphophobia in 1886 [7]. DSM-III listed it in 1980 as an atypical somatoform disorder, DSM-III-R renamed it body dysmorphic disorder in 1987, DSM-IV gave it formal criteria in 1994, and DSM-5 moved it to the obsessive-compulsive spectrum in 2013 [7].

Early clinical literature includes a 1993 American Journal of Psychiatry report of 30 cases of what the authors called imagined ugliness and a 1999 report of 33 children and adolescents [11][12]. A comparison of 34 people with BDD, 79 with OCD and 24 with both examined their features and comorbidity, reflecting long-standing discussion of how BDD relates to OCD [24].

Clinical reviews list mirror checking, camouflaging with makeup or clothing, excessive grooming, comparing, reassurance seeking and skin picking as typical associated behaviours, with some patients instead avoiding mirrors and social situations [2][4][5][6]. Wikipedia describes both repeated checking and mirror avoidance as signs of the disorder [7].

Cognitive-behavioural models propose that such behaviours, sometimes called safety behaviours, help maintain appearance concern. A randomised experiment with 84 undergraduate women who had elevated appearance concerns tested the effects of reducing appearance-related safety behaviours such as mirror checking and grooming on appearance concerns and related symptoms [10]. Wikipedia reports that the structured CBT manual by Sabine Wilhelm and colleagues includes exposure and ritual prevention [7].

Wikipedia describes body checking as repeatedly gathering information about size, shape, appearance or weight, with examples including mirror checking, pinching, measuring body parts and comparing one's body with others, and notes that it appears in eating disorders as well as BDD [17]. The article says checking brings short-term relief that reinforces the habit, while studies it cites link frequent checking to greater body dissatisfaction, and that research on body checking separate from eating disorders is rare [17].

Treatment approaches it lists include CBT, acceptance and commitment therapy and structured mirror exposure, with small studies reporting reduced checking [17]. It also explains the habit through upward social comparison, which social media can intensify, and through self-objectification, the tendency to judge self-worth by appearance [17].

A review in the Icelandic medical journal gives a weighted community prevalence of around 2%, higher in clinical, cosmetic and dermatology settings, with BDD usually beginning in childhood or adolescence and often co-occurring with depression, substance use disorders, social anxiety and obsessive-compulsive disorder [3]. Wikipedia cites a meta-analysis estimating general-population prevalence at about 17%, and notes that older estimates were 2 to 3 percent, so published figures differ by source and method [7].

Reviews report that BDD is frequently underdiagnosed because patients conceal symptoms out of shame, that insight is often poor, and that suicidal ideation and attempts are relatively common [3][5][6]. An early case series of 30 patients and a series of 33 children and adolescents documented its features [11][12].

Wikipedia describes a biopsychosocial model with genetic, developmental, psychological, social and cultural contributors, including childhood bullying or neglect, perfectionism, introversion and social anxiety, with one twin study estimating heritability at 43 percent [7]. A study published in the journal Body Image examined perceived teasing experiences in BDD [25].

Reviews on social media and body image describe how exposure to curated, idealised images is linked to body dissatisfaction in young people [26], and a 2025 dermatology review updates BDD concepts for an era of multiple social media platforms [19].

Muscle dysmorphia, in which a person believes their body is too small or insufficiently muscular, is a recognised subtype in DSM-5 and mostly affects men [7]. Published studies include a qualitative investigation of its phenomenology [13] and a report on posting muscle photos as a possible body-checking behaviour [14]. A multicentre study has examined BDD among patients with acne [15].

sections.h: Muscle dysmorphia in the gym context
paras: Wikipedia describes muscle dysmorphia as a subtype in which people believe their bodies are too small or insufficiently muscular despite often normal or muscular builds, with behaviours including heavy training, dietary restriction, supplements, anabolic steroid use and concealing the body under layers of clothing [18]. It was conceptualised in the 1990s, with Pope, Phillips and Olivardia publishing a 1997 paper on it as an underrecognised form of BDD, and DSM-5 classifies it under BDD [18]. Estimates in studied samples range widely, and rates are higher among gym members, bodybuilders and steroid users [18]. The same article says treatment evidence is mostly case reports, with family-based therapy, CBT and SSRIs having some support [18].

A guide for dermatologists and cosmetic surgeons reports that people with BDD often present to those practitioners, that preoccupation with skin, hair and nose is most common, and that reassurance seeking may be directed at clinicians [6]. Wikipedia says cosmetic treatment typically does not relieve the distress and recommends that surgeons and psychiatrists collaborate to screen candidates [7].

A 2024 review reports that the Australian regulator introduced a requirement that cosmetic surgery providers screen every potential patient for BDD with a validated tool, and identified six validated screening tools relevant to cosmetic practice, including the BDD Questionnaire Aesthetic Surgery version, which the authors' own practice adopted [20]. A systematic review of BDD in dermatology reported higher rates among dermatology patients than the background population and noted that people tend to seek help from non-mental-health specialists, so diagnosis can be delayed for years [21]. A 2024 editorial in JAAD International discusses the ethics of cosmetic overtreatment [27].

Human research on BDD is extensive; research specific to looksmaxxing communities is not. A randomised experiment tested reducing appearance-related safety behaviours in women with elevated appearance concerns [10]. Reviews state that cognitive behavioural therapy and serotonin reuptake inhibitors are most effective, and one reports that higher doses and longer trials than in depression are often needed [3][4]. No controlled studies found have examined mirror checking or BDD prevalence within looksmaxxing forums.

Wikipedia's article on looksmaxxing reports critics who describe the culture as demoralising and linked to body dysmorphia and suicidal ideation, as well as practitioners who report benefits such as dating success and peer affirmation [9]. Grokipedia also reports concern that self-rating and comparison, and fatalistic narratives about genetics, can deepen distress [8]. A 2026 analysis of dangerous facial-aesthetics trends on social media examined looksmaxxing discourse, though its abstract does not address BDD [16].

Forum users discuss the topic directly. In a looksmax.org thread, one member lists NHS-style BDD symptoms such as comparing looks, frequent mirror use or avoidance, concealment and skin picking, and says the list reads like a typical day for a looksmaxxer; replies in the thread dispute whether that amounts to BDD [22]. Another thread author describes leaving school and withdrawing from daily life, attributing it to concerns about his looks and to blackpill ideas [23].

Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article cites a BBC report from March 2024, a Guardian article from February 2024 and a Conversation article from January 2024 for the view that rating-focused communities can contribute to body dysmorphia, and also cites researchers who describe benefits some men report, such as dating success and peer praise [9]. Clinicians quoted in the sources describe BDD as treatable and underdiagnosed [3][5][6].

timeline.event: BDD recognised in DSM-III as an atypical somatoform disorder [7].
DSM revision renames it body dysmorphic disorder [7].
A report of 30 cases of imagined ugliness appears in the American Journal of Psychiatry [11].
DSM-IV gives BDD formal diagnostic criteria [7].
Pope, Phillips and Olivardia publish a paper on muscle dysmorphia as an underrecognised form of BDD [18].
A series of 33 children and adolescents with BDD is published [12].
DSM-5 moves BDD to the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders chapter and recognises muscle dysmorphia as a subtype [1][7].
A randomised experiment of 84 women tests fading appearance-related safety behaviours such as mirror checking [10].
Media coverage links looksmaxxing communities with body dysmorphia concerns; a review discusses mandatory BDD screening for cosmetic surgery patients in Australia [9][20].

lore.intro: Looksmaxxing forums discuss body dysmorphia both as a diagnosis people recognise in themselves and as a label some members say pathologises normal appearance concern [22][23]. Journalists and clinicians cited by Wikipedia discuss the overlap between rating culture and BDD [9].

claims.claim: Looksmaxxers' habits are normal, not BDD.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread author lists BDD symptoms and says they describe a day in the life of the average looksmaxxer; replies in the thread say everyone does these things [22].
claims.experts: Diagnosis requires preoccupation lasting hours a day with distress or impaired functioning, not scrutiny alone [3][7].

claims.claim: Checking and rating yourself shows what to fix.
claims.believers: Users treat frequent self-assessment, mirror use and photo comparison as part of the improvement process [22].
claims.experts: Cognitive-behavioural models say checking and grooming rituals maintain appearance concern, and a randomised experiment tested reducing them [10]; Wikipedia says checking gives short-term relief but is linked to more dissatisfaction over time [17].

claims.claim: Fixing the flaw will end the distress.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster describes his looks as the cause of withdrawing from school and social life [23].
claims.experts: Reviews report that people with BDD often seek cosmetic or dermatological treatment and that it often does not relieve the distress; surgeons and psychiatrists are advised to screen together [6][7][21].

claims.believers: Critics cited by Wikipedia say rating and comparison culture is linked to body dysmorphia and suicidal ideation [9].
claims.experts: Wikipedia and Grokipedia describe the concern, but no controlled study identified establishes how often BDD occurs in these communities or that they cause it [8][9].

claims.claim: Genetic fatalism ('it's over') worsens appearance distress.
claims.believers: Forum posts describe the blackpill as making appearance feel unfixable [23].
claims.experts: Grokipedia reports concern that self-rating and fatalistic narratives about genetics can deepen distress [8].

claims.believers: Clinicians and patient guides describe recovery with therapy.
claims.experts: Reviews describe CBT with exposure and ritual prevention and SSRIs as best supported, noting that higher doses and longer trials than in depression are often needed [3][4]; BDD is often underdiagnosed [5][6].

claims.claim: Muscle dysmorphia is a hidden risk in lifting communities.
claims.believers: Lifting and physique communities emphasise size, and users track muscle photos [14].
claims.experts: A report on posting muscle photos examines it as a possible body-checking behaviour, and Wikipedia reports higher rates among gym members and steroid users [14][18].

card.summary: Compulsive checking and appearance fixation: a recognised psychiatric condition (BDD) that clinicians say CBT and SSRIs can treat.
card.note: Reviews report high rates of suicidal ideation in BDD; resources exist through mental health professionals.

quick.overview:
Body dysmorphic disorder is a psychiatric condition in which a person spends hours on perceived flaws in their appearance that others barely notice. Mirror checking, comparing, reassurance seeking and camouflage are typical behaviours, and some people avoid mirrors instead.

Looksmaxxing communities involve heavy self-scrutiny, and critics cited by Wikipedia link the culture to body dysmorphia. No controlled study found establishes how often BDD occurs in these communities.
quick.mechanism: Clinical models treat checking and similar safety behaviours as maintaining appearance concern. Treatment research focuses on cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and ritual prevention, and on serotonin reuptake inhibitors.
quick.risks: Reviews report significant impairment, frequent comorbid depression and anxiety, and relatively common suicidal ideation. Cosmetic treatment typically does not relieve the distress, according to Wikipedia, and BDD is often underdiagnosed.

chain: Appearance scrutiny (mirror checking, comparing, rating) becomes frequent and time-consuming
Clinical models say checking and similar safety behaviours keep appearance concern going
Recognising the pattern and treating it (CBT, SSRIs) is reported to reduce distress and changes how people approach procedures and self-improvement
angle.text: Knowing the clinical picture helps people separate ordinary self-assessment from a pattern that clinicians treat, and reviews report that screening before cosmetic procedures is now required in some jurisdictions [20]. Reducing checking and comparison is the target of the main therapies described in the literature [7][17].
